why: A refresh that faults must end the inner sequence, not the outer subscription. Rethrowing kills the deferred-refresh stream permanently, so the list silently stops updating.
The whole point of the prefix clause. A revert costs the index and re-sorts the library, but produces a byte-identical query plan - only a structural assertion catches it.

why: The clause prefix and the index expression must agree. Changing one and not the other silently drops back to a full sort.
substr() returns a BINARY result and does not inherit the column collation, but bare c.content does. A NOCASE column leaves the two halves of the ORDER BY disagreeing.
Every sort needs its own pinned-prefixed index. Without one, the sort falls back to a temp B-tree over the whole library (252ms at 20k clips).
Same, for the expression index. Partial index coverage measured worse than none at all.

Compiling leniently on save lets an invalid pattern reach the database, which is the original bug: it was stored, then threw, and every later load threw on it too.
Strict compilation on load makes one bad stored pattern take down the entire rule set, leaving sensitivity scanning permanently unable to load.

why: App.OnSettingsChanged registers global hotkeys. RegisterHotKey binds WM_HOTKEY to the calling thread's message queue, so raising this from the pool kills every global hotkey silently until restart.
A deferred raise that reads the live field instead of the snapshot delivers the newest settings to every queued subscriber, so an earlier save is reported as the later one.
A view model that exposes ReactiveCommands but never calls ObserveCommandErrors leaves every failure in it silent. The IL-scan coverage test must catch that, or it is decoration.
If the reflection filter stops matching commands, ObserveCommandErrors silently subscribes to nothing and the coverage test passes vacuously for every view model.
Reporting must reach the installed sink; dropping to the Trace fallback while a sink exists leaves the user with no status message.
ReactiveObject also implements IHandleObservableErrors, so the looser filter matches every nested view-model property and double-reports their command failures.
Marking every dispatcher exception handled lets the app keep writing to the clip database after a failure that leaves managed state undefined.
Without a notification the user cannot tell a failed action from one that silently did nothing, which is the whole defect.
A fatal cause usually arrives wrapped in an AggregateException or a rethrow; only checking the outer type lets it through.
InsufficientMemoryException derives from OutOfMemoryException but is thrown before allocating, so it is recoverable; killing the app on it loses the user's session for nothing.
Without the rollback, any failure after the stash leaves the live path empty and the user's history under a .before-restore name that nothing looks for.
Stashing only the main file leaves stale -wal/-shm beside a different database, which SQLite may replay into it.
File.Move refuses an existing destination, so failing to clear the half-restored file makes the rollback a no-op.
The .before-restore copy is the user's only undo for a restore they did not mean to run; deleting the live files instead of renaming them destroys it.

Reverts the daily backup to a raw file copy. A checkpoint that cannot finish leaves committed frames in the WAL, and the copied .db then opens as 'database disk image is malformed' - an unopenable backup nobody notices until they need it.
Reverts the database path move to a raw file copy. The source is deleted immediately after the rename, so anything the copy missed is gone.
Writes the destination unencrypted. The copy would then be readable by anyone with the file, and unreadable by the app that expects the live key.
Leaves the connections in the pool, so the copied file is still held open and the caller's move or delete fails.
A truncated or differently-keyed leftover file at the destination cannot be opened, so failing to clear it first blocks every future copy to that path - backups stop happening and nothing says so.
find:
// and would block every future copy to this path, so clear it.
        File.Delete(destinationPath);
replace:
// and would block every future copy to this path, so clear it.
        _ = destinationPath;

why: Puts the column-dependent indexes back in the DDL batch that runs before the Ensure*Columns helpers. The batch then aborts with 'no such column' on any database predating those columns, so the app cannot open the user's history.

Skips the sort-order indexes entirely. They only work as a complete set - with partial coverage SQLite picks a pinned-prefixed index for an uncovered sort and fetches rows in an uncorrelated order, measured slower than no index at all.
byte_size was declared in CREATE TABLE but never added by a migration, so databases older than the column never gained it and could not be opened once an index referenced it.
The migration helpers are skipped when the stored version already matches, so new migration work is dead code unless the constant is bumped. Existing databases would silently never gain byte_size.
Puts index creation behind the schema-version gate, so an index dropped or lost on an up-to-date database is never restored - queries silently fall back to a scan.

Restores writing storage.json before flipping Current. A path move has already deleted the source by then, so a failed write leaves Current naming a path with no database - the workers restart there, create an empty one, and the real history is orphaned.

Flips Current before persisting even when nothing moved. A config-only write that fails then leaves the running session using settings that were never saved, silently diverging from what the next launch will read.

Restores joining whole-word tokens into one alternation. Ticking 'whole word' then silently turns a two-word AND search into an OR and returns clips containing either word, while the plain-text and FTS paths for the same query still require both.

Restores fusing the globally-ranked semantic top-K into every paged read. Load more is then handed the same semantic hits it already showed and appends them again, so a clip gets two view models whose selection and checkbox state diverge.

Restores paging on the on-screen row count. Semantic additions are not part of the query's offset space, so counting them advances the offset past query rows that were never shown - those clips match the search and appear on no page at all.

Stops clearing the semantic-addition mark when the query itself returns the clip on a later page. The offset then stays one row short for good, so every further Load more re-reads a row already on screen, discards it as a duplicate, and the list never grows again.

Restores trimming the fused page back to the page size. The lowest-ranked query rows are dropped to make room for semantic additions, and the next page resumes past them - so clips that matched the search are shown on no page.

Removes the call that syncs the embedding worker with the EnableSemanticSearch setting. Toggling semantic search then does nothing until the next launch: on leaves clips unembedded, off leaves the worker running.
Drops the disable branch, so turning semantic search off leaves the embedding worker running and consuming CPU and the SQLite write lock.

Runs each start/stop transition independently instead of chaining it onto the previous one. A rapid off->on toggle can then let the pending stop land after the start, leaving the worker off while semantic search is enabled.

Restores the unconditional restart in DatabaseMaintenanceScope.DisposeAsync. A worker the user had deliberately turned off (capture paused, semantic search disabled) comes back to life after any whole-database operation.
